assignments.title: 19.7 Quarter 3 Capstone: The Road to War
assignments.html:
QUARTER 3 CAPSTONE
The Road to War
One essay on the years from the Marne to Poland.
Capstone · 20 points · Word document upload
☂ ─ ☂ ─ ☂
HOW TO WORK
Read your notes in My Notebook and look back over the quarter's lessons and primary sources first. Then write your essay in Word and submit it as the submission box below describes.
WHAT YOU ARE DOING

The Quarter 3 Capstone is one essay that brings the whole quarter together, from the Marne in 1914 to the invasion of Poland in 1939. You will choose one of three questions, make an argument, and defend it with evidence from the lessons and the primary sources you have read.

CHOOSE ONE QUESTION
  1. Was the Second World War made at Versailles, or by the decisions of the 1930s?
  2. Between 1919 and 1939, did free governments fall mainly because of weak institutions, or because of the choices of particular men?
  3. Between 1931 and 1939, was there a moment when war could still have been prevented? If so, when, and who would have had to act?
WHAT YOUR ESSAY MUST DO

Write 800 to 1,200 words in Word. Give your essay a title. State your answer in the first paragraph, and keep it clear to the end.

  1. Use specific evidence from at least four different weeks of the quarter, naming people, decisions, and dates.
  2. Quote from at least two of the primary sources of the quarter. Put each quotation in quotation marks and cite it in a footnote.
  3. Include one counterfactual. Name a moment, say what might have gone differently, and say what you think would have followed.
  4. Answer the strongest objection to your view. Say what a thoughtful person on the other side would point to, and why you are still not persuaded.
  5. Say plainly what the evidence cannot show and what you are guessing.

You will be graded on the quality of your argument, not on which question you choose or which side you take.

HOW TO SUBMIT

Write your essay in Word and save it to your OneDrive folder. Then open this assignment in Canvas, choose the OneDrive tab, select your file, and submit.

M365 reminder: name your file like this: LastName_FirstName_Q3Capstone_WHSP. Save it in Optima → History → WorldHistory_Spring. Name your sources in footnotes (M365 Skill You’re Practicing: Inserting a Footnote in Word).

If you chose to work with a group in the module introduction, submit one shared essay and list every group member’s name under the title. Otherwise, write alone. Both paths use the same rubric.

MODULE INTRODUCTION
Module Introduction: The Road to War: Quarter 3 Capstone
Survey · 3 questions · not graded
☂ ─ ☂ ─ ☂
Before you start

Welcome to The Road to War: Quarter 3 Capstone. Answer the questions below before you open the first lesson. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting. This survey is not graded.

This module's goals:
  • Describe Hitler’s steps from the Rhineland to Munich and explain why Britain and France did not stop him.
  • Explain how the seizure of Prague, the pledge to Poland, and the Nazi-Soviet Pact led to war.
  • Weigh whether Munich bought time or cost it, and bring the quarter together in your Capstone.

questions.text: Before you read: Did Munich buy time or cost it? Give your first answer in two or three sentences. You will answer it again at the end of the module, so it is fine if your answer changes.
I have read this module's goals and I know what I am working toward this week.

answers.text: Yes, I have read them
Not yet, I will read them before the first lesson

questions.text: You may do this week’s main assignment alone or with a group. If you choose a group, you agree to the Group Covenant and to submit one shared piece. Which do you choose?

answers.text: I will work alone
I will work with a group and I agree to the Group Covenant

quizzes.title: 19.10 Quarter 3 Exam
quizzes.description:
QUARTER EXAM
Quarter 3 Exam
Exam · 20 questions · 40 points
☂ ─ ☂ ─ ☂
Before you start

This exam covers Quarter 3 only. It has 20 multiple-choice questions worth 2 points each, 40 points in all. Read each question carefully and choose the best answer.

HOW TO WORK
Look back over the quarter's lessons and primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then answer the questions below.

questions.text: Why did German planners want to beat France quickly and then turn east?

answers.text: Russia had agreed to stay neutral if Germany attacked France
France had the weakest army of Germany’s enemies and could be beaten in days
Russia needed weeks to mobilize, so Germany could win in the west first
Britain had promised to defend France but not to defend Russia

questions.text: On September 2, 1914, General von Kluck turned southeast and passed east of Paris. What did this do?

answers.text: It exposed his flank to the French army gathering in Paris
It cut the French army off from the sea and trapped it
It brought the Germans to the gates of Paris within a day
It forced the British army to leave the continent

questions.text: Why did the Allies attack the Dardanelles and Gallipoli in 1915?

answers.text: To capture Constantinople as a base for striking Germany directly
To break the German blockade of the North Sea ports
To protect the Suez Canal from a German fleet in the Red Sea
To knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war and open a sea road to Russia

questions.text: What does “Mobilizing Whole Peoples: Propaganda and the Home Front” say about the Bryce Report of 1915?

answers.text: Every story in the report was later proved false by the historians who studied it
It was based on real killings, but some of its worst stories had weak evidence
It was written by the German government to answer the charges the Allies made
It was kept secret by the British government until after the war had ended

questions.text: Why did the Zimmermann Telegram turn American opinion against Germany?

answers.text: It announced that German submarines would soon begin attacking American ports and ships
It offered Mexico help to win back Texas and other lands, and Zimmermann admitted it
It showed that Britain had broken the American diplomatic code and read its secrets
It asked the United States to stay out of the war in return for peace

questions.text: What did the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk cost Russia?

answers.text: Only its ports on the Black Sea and the right to use the straits
Its alliance with France and Britain, but not any land
Its army, which Germany forced the Bolsheviks to disband
Poland, the Baltic lands, Ukraine, and a third of its people

questions.text: What did Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles say?

answers.text: Germany and its allies were responsible for all loss and damage
Germany must give up its army and destroy all its factories
Germany could never join the League of Nations
Germany would pay for the war only if it fought another

questions.text: Why did the United States Senate refuse to approve the Treaty of Versailles?

answers.text: The Senate thought the treaty was too easy on Germany and wanted to continue the war
The Senate voted for the treaty, but the House of Representatives voted against it
Senators feared Article 10 could send soldiers to war without a vote of Congress, and Wilson would not bargain
Most senators opposed the treaty because it had no League of Nations in it

questions.text: What was John Maynard Keynes’s main argument in The Economic Consequences of the Peace?

answers.text: The treaty should have been harsher so that Germany could never fight again
Germany should have kept its colonies in order to pay its debts
The League of Nations should have been given the job of collecting reparations
The reparations were too large to pay and would drag down all of Europe

questions.text: Why was Mussolini able to take power in October 1922?

answers.text: The army joined the Blackshirts and overthrew the King and the government
The King would not use the army against the march and asked Mussolini to lead
Mussolini won a majority in a free national election held that same month
Parliament voted him emergency powers in order to end the strikes and riots

questions.text: Who suffered most from the German hyperinflation of 1923, according to “Inflation, Crash, and Two Answers: Weimar and Roosevelt's America”?

answers.text: People who had saved for years, such as retired teachers
Factory owners who had borrowed heavily from the banks to build new works
Farmers who had paid off their loans in worthless paper money
Government officials, who were paid in gold coins

questions.text: In his postscript of January 4, 1923, what did Lenin say about Stalin?

answers.text: He should become the next leader of the party after Lenin’s death
He should be sent to lead the Red Army against the Whites
He was too rude and should be replaced as General Secretary by a more patient man
He should be tried for his actions in the civil war

questions.text: Why did the poor harvest of 1932 become a famine that killed millions?

answers.text: Stalin ordered the peasants to plant only cotton and tobacco for export
Foreign nations refused to sell any food to the Soviet Union at that time
The kulaks hid all of the grain in the cities and towns of the country
The state kept its grain quotas and seized seed and food from villages

questions.text: How did the vote on the Enabling Act of March 23, 1933, pass?

answers.text: Every party except the Nazis in the Reichstag voted for the law
Communist deputies were jailed or in hiding, SA men stood outside, and the Center Party voted yes
Hindenburg signed it as a decree without any vote at all
The Social Democrats voted for it after Hitler promised free elections

questions.text: How did Hitler become Chancellor on January 30, 1933?

answers.text: Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint him, believing he could be controlled
He won a majority of the votes in a free national election held in November 1932
He overthrew the government with the SA in a single night of street fighting
Hindenburg resigned from office and named him both president and Chancellor

questions.text: Why did Mao’s Communists begin the Long March in October 1934?

answers.text: Soviet advisers ordered them to move their army into Manchuria
Japan had attacked their base in Jiangxi and driven them out
Chiang’s forts cut off their food and the Jiangxi Soviet began to starve
They hoped to reach Nanjing before the Nationalists could

questions.text: What do we now know about the bomb on the railway near Mukden in September 1931?

answers.text: Chinese soldiers set it, just as the Japanese government said
Japanese officers set it themselves as an excuse to attack
Soviet agents set it to start a war in Manchuria
It was an accident that the army then used as an excuse

questions.text: Who was NOT invited to the Munich conference of September 1938?

answers.text: Britain and France, whose leaders were the hosts of the meeting
Italy and Germany, whose leaders had called the meeting
Poland and Romania, whose borders were being redrawn
Czechoslovakia and the Soviet Union, whose fate was being decided

questions.text: Why did Stalin sign the Nazi-Soviet Pact in August 1939?

answers.text: He distrusted the West after Munich and wanted time to build up his army
He had agreed to join Hitler in an attack on Britain
He wanted to halt the German advance into Ukraine
The League of Nations had asked him to make peace with Germany

questions.text: Britain’s promise to defend Poland in March 1939 was remarkable. Why?

answers.text: Britain had no navy that could reach any port on the coast of Poland
Poland had not asked Britain or France for any help in the crisis
Britain had never before guaranteed borders in eastern Europe, and had no army to send
It was the first treaty that Britain had ever signed with France or Poland

discussions.title: 19.8 Discussion: Did Munich buy time or cost it?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Did Munich buy time or cost it?
A year of preparation, or the loss of an ally's army and forts?
Graded discussion · 10 points · one post and one reply
☂ ─ ☂ ─ ☂
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then post your answer to the prompt below, and reply to one classmate.
DISCUSSION PROMPT

This week’s question: Did Munich buy time or cost it?

Choose a side. Name at least one thing Britain and France gained at Munich and at least one thing they lost, and say which weighs more. Use at least one fact from “The Nazi-Soviet Pact and the Invasion of Poland” about what Hitler did with the year.

Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Then add one sentence on courage. Some at the time called Munich prudence and some called it fear. Which word fits, and why?

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a fact or decision they did not use. If not, say politely where you think it falls short, and give your reason.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
CriteriaSubstantive (full credit)Thin (partial credit)Missing (no credit)
Your claim and your reasons
6 pts		Takes a clear side, uses the specific evidence the prompt asks for, and explains why it supports the claim.Takes a side but gives general reasons, or leaves out part of what the prompt asks for.No post, or no claim.
Your reply to a classmate
4 pts		Answers one classmate's actual reasoning. Strengthens it or says where it falls short, politely and with a reason.Replies, but only to agree or disagree with no reason.No reply.
10 pts total
